items.prompt: How does the writer tell the reader what happened in 1968?

options.text: The story begins in 1968 and moves forward.
options.why: The story begins with Bayu finding the map, many years later.

options.text: Nenek explains it to the children after they find the tin.
Laila reads about it in a diary.
options.why: There is no diary in the story.

options.text: Laila remembers being there.

hints: The story is told in the present, but part of it is about the past.
Look for the paragraph that begins She told us.
Ask: who knows what happened in 1968?
items.explanation: The past is revealed when Nenek tells the children about burying the tin with her friends. This lets the reader learn the history at the same time as Laila.

items.prompt: Match each year to what happened.
pairs: He wrote “If I Were a Dutchman”.
He returned home from the Netherlands.
He became the first Minister of Education.
hints: A biography usually gives events in time order.
Scan the text for each year.
Start with the earliest year. What happened then?
items.explanation: The biography follows Ki Hajar Dewantara’s life in time order, from his birth in 1889 to his death in 1959.

items.prompt: Choose all the features of a biography that this text has.

options.text: It is written in the third person, using he and his.
Events are mostly in time order.
It is written by Ki Hajar Dewantara himself.
It includes dates and real places.
It uses rhyme and rhythm.
options.why: Rhyme and rhythm are features of poems.

options.text: It gives step-by-step instructions.
options.why: Instructions are a different type of text.

hints: Think about what makes a biography different from other texts.
A biography is the story of a real person’s life, written by someone else.
Check the pronouns, the order and the facts in the text.
items.explanation: Biographies are written in the third person, usually follow time order and include real dates and places.

items.prompt: How can you tell that this text is a balanced argument?

options.text: It only gives reasons to support the idea.
options.why: It also includes the worries of shop owners and drivers.

options.text: It tells the story of one family’s Sunday.
It gives arguments for and against before the writer’s conclusion.
It gives instructions for planning a Car Free Day.
options.why: It discusses the idea rather than giving instructions.

hints: Look at what each paragraph is about.
Some paragraphs support the idea. Look for where the other side begins.
Find the word However. What comes after it?
items.explanation: The text gives the supporters’ arguments, then the worries against the idea, and only then gives the writer’s view. This is the shape of a balanced argument.

items.prompt: Sort the points into arguments for and against the car-free road.
hints: Some points come from supporters and some from people who are worried.
The arguments against come after the word However.
Start with the air would be cleaner. Is that a reason for or against?
items.explanation: Exercise, cleaner air and friendlier neighbours are arguments for the idea. Lost customers, longer routes and traffic jams are arguments against it.

items.prompt: Put the steps that cause the wet season in order.
items: The air over hot Australia rises.
Wind blows from Asia towards Australia.
The wind picks up water vapour over warm seas.
The moist air reaches Indonesia and rises.
The air cools and forms thick clouds.
Heavy rain falls on islands such as Java.
hints: An explanation often describes a chain of causes and effects.
Find the paragraph about December to February and follow it sentence by sentence.
Start with what happens to the air over Australia.
items.explanation: Rising air over Australia draws wind from Asia. The wind gathers water vapour over the sea, then the moist air rises over Indonesia, cools into clouds and falls as rain.

items.prompt: Read the paragraph about June to August. Find and copy the connective that starts a sentence and means as a result.
hints: Find the paragraph that begins From around June to August.
Look at the first word of each sentence in that paragraph.
You need a word that shows an effect or result.
items.explanation: Consequently means as a result. It shows that the dry season is caused by the dry wind from Australia.

items.prompt: The opening paragraph of a news report often answers who, what and where. Read the paragraph below the reporter’s name. Which question does it not answer?

options.text: What has happened?
options.why: It says a boat of books has begun regular visits.

options.text: Where are the islands?
options.why: It says they are off the coast of Sulawesi.

options.text: Who benefits from the project?
options.why: It says hundreds of children benefit.

options.text: Who leads the project?

hints: Read only the first paragraph, under the reporter’s name.
Check each question against that paragraph.
Is anybody named in the first paragraph?
items.explanation: The opening paragraph tells us what happened, where and who benefits. The leader, Pak Haris Mandala, is named only in the next paragraph.

items.prompt: Which is the best summary of the whole report?

options.text: A retired teacher found some damaged books on an island two years ago.
options.why: This is only one detail from the background.

options.text: Rough seas in the wet season stop boats from sailing.
options.why: This is one challenge, not the main point.

options.text: Children on the islands like animal books more than any other books.
options.why: Only one girl is mentioned, so this is not the main idea.

options.text: Volunteers have started a boat library for island children, and it is helping them read more, despite problems with weather and damp.

hints: A summary covers the main points of the whole text.
Check that the summary includes what happened, the effect and the problems.
Cross out any option that only describes one detail or one person.
items.explanation: The best summary includes the main event, the effect on children and the challenges. The other options each describe only one detail.
